The Goldblotch grouper Epinephelus costae displays a life history strategy characteristic of large-bodied serranids inhabiting Mediterranean and eastern Atlantic waters. Field studies indicate that newly emerged prolarvae, hatching from pelagic eggs with a recorded egg diameter of 0.8 mm, possess an extremely modest wet weight at birth of approximately 0.000268 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000268 grams]. This minuscule initial mass reflects the energetically constrained yolk reserves available to the lecithotrophic yolk-sac larva. The larval phase is prolonged and entirely pelagic, with the exotrophic transition occurring after the complete absorption of endogenous nutrients. As the free-swimming larva grows and develops through the flexion and postflexion stages, it gradually accumulates somatic tissue. The eventual attainment of the adult body plan is marked by metamorphosis and subsequent settlement into demersal habitats, after which the juvenile fish enters a phase of rapid somatic growth that will ultimately define its maximum adult body size.

Comparisons with congeneric species highlight the substantial asymptotic size reached by Epinephelus costae. The ultimate total length of this species has been recorded at 140 centimeters [Li = 140 centimeters], a value that places it among the larger members of the genus. This considerable length corresponds to an ultimate wet weight estimated at 24,000 grams [Wwi = 24,000 grams], based on length-weight relationships derived from captured specimens. Such a large body mass is associated with a comparatively slow life history pace. The species is known to be long-lived, with the maximum recorded lifespan in the wild reaching 21 years [am = 21 years] under the thermal conditions typical of its subtropical range, where mean annual water temperatures approximate 19 °C [T = 19 °C]. This extended longevity is consistent with the delayed maturation and iteroparous reproductive strategy observed in many large epinephelids that face relatively low natural mortality once they reach adult size.

Reproductive development in this grouper follows a distinct pattern linked to body size rather than chronological age alone. The total length at puberty, marking the onset of gonadal maturation, has been determined from histological examination of captured individuals to be 32.5 centimeters [Lp = 32.5 centimeters]. Fish attaining this length typically have a corresponding wet weight at puberty of approximately 296 grams [Wwp = approximately 296 grams]. The transition from the immature juvenile stage to a reproductively active adult involves significant activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, initiating vitellogenesis in females and spermiation in males. Although the species is a protogynous hermaphrodite, the initial maturation event for individuals functioning as females occurs at this size threshold. Growth continues steadily after puberty, as the fish allocate resources toward both somatic expansion and the production of gametes during the annual spawning season.

Reproductive output in Epinephelus costae is substantial, reflecting the high fecundity typical of batch-spawning serranids. During a single spawning event, a gravid female releases a large number of pelagic oocytes. Based on fecundity estimates derived from closely related species such as Epinephelus bleekeri, the maximum reproductive rate has been calculated to involve the production of approximately 2,740 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 2,740 eggs per day] under optimal thermal conditions recorded at 19 °C [T = 19 °C]. This daily rate of egg production is sustained over the course of the spawning season, during which females may release multiple batches of eggs. The high per capita fecundity is an adaptive response to the extreme mortality experienced during the early pelagic larval phase, where survival from the yolk-sac stage to juvenile recruitment is typically very low. Such a life history strategy prioritizes numerical output over parental investment in individual offspring.

The ecological niche occupied by adult Goldblotch groupers is that of a demersal, benthic-feeding predator inhabiting rocky reefs and seagrass beds. Their ultimate wet weight of 24,000 grams [Wwi = 24,000 grams] and ultimate total length of 140 centimeters [Li = 140 centimeters] allow them to take relatively large prey, including crustaceans, cephalopods, and demersal fishes. The extended lifespan of 21 years [am = 21 years] provides a lengthy reproductive window, enabling multiple spawning seasons over the course of an individual's life at a temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C]. Field observations suggest that the species exhibits site fidelity to specific reef structures, which may be important for both foraging and spawning aggregation formation. The combination of late sexual maturation, high fecundity, and long lifespan aligns well with the life history strategy of a slow-growing, large-bodied marine teleost that experiences relatively stable adult mortality rates.
